sections.heading: Clients and servers: who does what
paragraphs: The web is a conversation between two roles. A client (usually a browser) asks for things. A server listens on a network address, receives those requests, and answers. Neither side keeps a phone line open — every exchange is a discrete request followed by a discrete response.

This matters because HTTP is stateless: the server does not inherently remember your previous request. Anything that feels like memory — being logged in, a shopping cart, a half-filled form — is rebuilt on every request from data the client sends along (cookies, tokens) or data the server looks up (a database keyed by the identity in that cookie). The protocol carries no thread of continuity; the application weaves one.

This division of labor is the mental model everything else hangs on. When an interviewer asks 'what happens when you type a URL and press Enter', this request/response boundary is the backbone of the answer — and every later topic (caching, sessions, CORS, REST) is a rule about how one side asks or the other side answers.
sections.summary: The web forgets between requests, so anything that feels like memory is rebuilt each time from what the client sends along.

variants.question: HTTP is described as a *stateless* protocol. What does that actually mean?
options: Each request stands alone; the server keeps no built-in memory of a client's past requests
The client may only receive data from the server and can never send any of its own back
Application state is allowed to live on the client, but it may never be stored on the server
The server crashes outright if it ever tries to store any data in between two requests
variants.rationale: Statelessness means the protocol itself carries no memory between requests. Each request must contain everything needed to handle it — which is exactly why cookies, sessions, and tokens exist: they re-introduce continuity on top of a stateless protocol.
optionExplanations: Correct — the protocol has no built-in memory; continuity is layered on with cookies, sessions, or tokens.
Clients send data all the time — form submissions, JSON bodies, uploaded files. That has nothing to do with statelessness.
Servers absolutely store state (that is what databases are). The protocol just doesn't carry it between requests automatically.
Servers store data constantly (databases, caches). Statelessness is a property of the protocol, not a restriction on server storage.
variants.interviewTip: A favorite follow-up is 'so how does login work over a stateless protocol?' Be ready to explain cookies and session/token round-tripping in one breath.

variants.question: You load a product page, then reload it a second later while logged in, and the server still 'knows' you and your cart. Given that HTTP is stateless, how does the server actually recognize you on that second request?
options: The server holds a persistent open connection to your browser and reads your identity straight off it
The reload re-sends a `Cookie` header or token that the server uses to look you up again
Statelessness applies only to the first request; every request after it is automatically stateful
The browser stamps each request with a permanent trusted hardware ID that the server reads off
variants.rationale: Because the protocol remembers nothing, the *client* must re-present its identity on every single request — typically a session cookie or bearer token the server uses to re-load your session and cart from storage. Continuity is rebuilt each time, not preserved by the protocol.
optionExplanations: HTTP does not hold an open identity-bearing line; even keep-alive TCP connections carry independent, self-contained requests with no inherent memory of who you are.
Correct — the client re-sends a cookie or token on every request, and the server re-derives your identity and cart from it.
Statelessness applies to every request equally; there is no 'first request' exception that flips the protocol into a stateful mode.
Browsers send no permanent trusted hardware ID; identity rides in cookies/tokens the app issues, precisely because the protocol itself carries none.
variants.interviewTip: Turn it around: 'the protocol forgets, so the client must remind it every request.' Naming the exact carrier — cookie or Authorization header — shows you know where the continuity physically lives.

variants.question: Your team adds a second app server behind a load balancer. A teammate objects: 'users who logged in through server 1 will break the moment the balancer routes their next request to server 2.' Under stateless HTTP, what actually determines whether this works?
options: It cannot work, because HTTP permanently pins each authenticated client to the server that first saw it
It works on its own, because the load balancer mirrors each server's memory to the other in real time
It works if every request carries its credential and session data lives in storage any server can read
It works only if users are forced to log in again whenever the balancer switches which server they hit
variants.rationale: Statelessness is exactly why horizontal scaling works: each request is self-contained, carrying its own credential, so any server can handle it — provided the session lookup hits shared storage (a database, Redis) rather than one machine's RAM. The teammate's fear is only valid if session state was trapped in server 1's memory.
optionExplanations: HTTP pins nothing; there is no protocol-level binding between a client and a server. 'Sticky sessions' exist as a load-balancer workaround, not an HTTP rule.
Load balancers route packets; they do not replicate application memory. Any real-time memory mirroring would be an application architecture choice, not balancer magic.
Correct — self-contained requests plus shared session storage means any server can answer any request, which is the payoff of building on a stateless protocol.
No re-login is needed: the same cookie or token travels with every request regardless of which server receives it, and each server can validate it independently.
variants.interviewTip: If someone proposes sticky sessions, name the trade-off: they paper over in-memory session state but break the moment a server dies. Externalizing sessions to Redis or a database is the answer interviewers want to hear.

variants.question: A junior dev inspects a response, sees `Connection: keep-alive`, and concludes: 'HTTP isn't really stateless — the server is holding our connection open, so it must be remembering us.' What is wrong with that reasoning?
options: Keep-alive reuses the TCP connection to skip handshakes; the requests over it stay independent
Nothing is wrong — keep-alive was introduced precisely to turn HTTP into a stateful protocol
Keep-alive does persist your session, but only over HTTPS where the TLS layer quietly stores it
The header is purely informational and has no real effect on how the connection is handled at all
variants.rationale: Statelessness lives at the level of protocol semantics, not transport plumbing. Keep-alive (and HTTP/2 multiplexing) reuses the expensive TCP/TLS setup for performance, but each request over that connection must still be fully self-describing — the server derives nothing about your identity from the socket itself.
optionExplanations: Correct — connection reuse is a transport optimization; every request over the reused socket is still processed as an independent, self-contained unit.
Keep-alive exists to amortize handshake cost, not to add memory. HTTP's request/response semantics are unchanged by it.
TLS secures the channel; it does not store application sessions, and keep-alive behaves the same with or without HTTPS.
The header genuinely governs connection reuse (especially in HTTP/1.x) — it just has no bearing on whether the server remembers you.
variants.interviewTip: Separating layers cleanly — 'TCP reuse is performance, statelessness is semantics' — is a strong systems signal. It also sets up a natural segue to HTTP/2 multiplexing if the interviewer wants to go deeper.

sections.heading: Anatomy of an HTTP request
paragraphs: An HTTP request is plain structured text with three parts. First a request line — a method and path (`GET /products/42 HTTP/1.1`). Then headers: key-value metadata like `Accept: application/json` (what the client wants back), `Content-Type: application/json` (what the body is), or `Cookie: session=abc` (who the client is). Then, optionally, a body — the payload, present on `POST`/`PUT`/`PATCH` and empty on a plain `GET`.

The method declares intent, and picking the right one is a design decision, not a formality. `GET` reads and should never change anything. `POST` creates or triggers an action. `PUT` replaces a resource entirely, `PATCH` updates part of it, and `DELETE` removes it. Servers, proxies, and browsers all trust these meanings, so a method that lies about its intent invites subtle bugs.

Two properties sharpen the choice. A method is *safe* if it has no side effects (`GET`, `HEAD`) — the whole web assumes safe methods are free to fire speculatively. A method is *idempotent* if repeating it leaves the same final state: `GET`, `PUT`, and `DELETE` qualify, so they can be safely retried after a timeout. `POST` is neither, which is why your bank warns you not to click 'Pay' twice — real payment APIs add an idempotency key to make retries safe.
sections.summary: Each request states its intent through its method, and picking the right one decides whether a retry is safe or repeats the action.

variants.question: A payment API endpoint charges a card when called. A flaky network means the client may retry requests automatically. Which method choice best reflects HTTP semantics for 'create a new charge'?
options: GET, since it is the simplest method and the easiest to test directly in a browser
PUT, since a charge should be freely retryable and PUT is safe to repeat blindly
POST, with the server using an idempotency key to de-duplicate any retried charge
DELETE, since charging a card ultimately removes money from the customer's account
variants.rationale: Creating a new resource is POST's job. Since POST is not idempotent, real payment APIs (like Stripe) let the client send an idempotency key so a retried POST doesn't create a second charge — the semantics stay honest and retries stay safe.
optionExplanations: GET must never cause side effects. Browsers, proxies, and prefetchers freely repeat GETs — a GET that charges money could fire from a link preview.
PUT means 'replace the resource at this URL with this body'. A new charge has no URL yet, and blind retry-safety without an idempotency scheme is exactly the trap.
Correct — POST for creation, plus an idempotency key to make retries safe in practice.
DELETE removes the resource identified by the URL. Charging money is creating a charge record, not deleting anything.
variants.interviewTip: Mentioning idempotency keys when discussing POST retries is a strong signal you've thought about real-world API failure modes.

variants.question: A mobile app lets a user edit their whole profile by sending the full profile object to `/users/42/profile`. If the request times out and the app silently re-sends the identical body, which method makes that automatic retry inherently safe — no duplicate side effects — without any extra de-duplication logic?
options: `PATCH`, because a partial update is always safe to apply repeatedly by definition
`GET`, because reads can be repeated freely and this is really just fetching data
`POST`, because it is the standard verb whenever you need to send a body of data
`PUT`, because replacing the resource with the same body twice leaves it unchanged
variants.rationale: `PUT` replaces the resource at a known URL with the supplied representation. Applying the identical replacement twice yields the same final state as applying it once — that is idempotency, so a blind retry is safe without an idempotency key. The resource already has a URL (`/users/42/profile`), which is exactly what `PUT` requires.
optionExplanations: `PATCH` is not guaranteed idempotent — a partial update like 'increment balance by 10' applied twice diverges; safety depends on the patch's semantics, not the method.
`GET` is safe to repeat but it only reads; it cannot perform the profile edit the scenario requires, so it is the wrong tool entirely.
`POST` is not idempotent; a re-sent `POST` may create a second record or re-trigger an action, so an automatic retry is unsafe by default.
Correct — `PUT` is a full replacement to a known URL; repeating the same replacement leaves identical state, so the retry is inherently safe.
variants.interviewTip: Don't lump `PATCH` in with `PUT` as 'both safe to retry' — `PATCH` is idempotent only if the patch itself is. That distinction is a common trap.

variants.question: A client sends `DELETE /orders/99` and receives `204 No Content`. A network-layer retry re-sends the identical request and gets `404 Not Found`. A teammate declares: 'see — different responses, so `DELETE` isn't actually idempotent.' Are they right?
options: Yes — an idempotent method must, by definition, return the very same status code on every repetition
No — idempotency is about resulting server state, not identical responses; the order is gone either way
Yes — the `404` on retry proves the second request corrupted the server state the first had left intact
No — but only because the server silently suppressed the second delete; a real one would break idempotency
variants.rationale: Idempotency means N identical requests leave the server in the same state as one request. The order is deleted after the first call and still deleted after the retry — state is unchanged. The differing status codes are just the server truthfully describing what it found each time; nothing in the spec requires repeat responses to match.
optionExplanations: The spec defines idempotency in terms of the effect on the server, not the response. `DELETE` then `404` on retry is the textbook-compliant behavior.
Correct — same final state ('order 99 does not exist') after one call or ten; the response merely reports what the server found at that moment.
Nothing was corrupted: the `404` reflects that the resource was already gone, which is exactly the state the first `DELETE` produced.
The server executed both requests honestly; the second simply found nothing to delete. No suppression mechanism is needed for `DELETE` to be idempotent.
variants.interviewTip: Define idempotency precisely — 'same server state after N calls as after 1' — before answering retry questions. Interviewers plant the differing-response red herring specifically to see if your definition is about state or about responses.

variants.question: A team ships `GET /reports/latest/regenerate`, which rebuilds an expensive report and emails it to stakeholders whenever it is hit. Weeks later, stakeholders complain about duplicate report emails arriving at odd hours when nobody was using the app. What is the root design flaw?
options: The URL is too long, which causes some intermediary proxies to replay the request on their own
Regeneration replaces the old report file, so the endpoint should have been `PUT` to stay idempotent
`GET` responses get cached by intermediaries, and the duplicate emails are being sent from those caches
`GET` must be safe, but prefetchers, crawlers, and monitors fire GETs on their own; it should be `POST`
variants.rationale: The entire web infrastructure — browser prefetching, link previews in chat apps, search crawlers, uptime monitors — assumes GETs are safe to issue speculatively and repeatedly. Hang a side effect (regenerating, emailing) off a GET and that machinery triggers it invisibly. State-changing actions belong on `POST` (or another non-safe method) precisely so automated agents leave them alone.
optionExplanations: URL length has nothing to do with replays; well-behaved intermediaries repeat GETs because GETs are declared safe, regardless of URL size.

`PUT` would make the *state change* retry-safe, but the email dispatch is a side effect no method makes idempotent — and the real bug is that automated agents trigger the endpoint at all, which switching to `PUT` alone doesn't fully stop since the deeper contract violated is safety.
Caches store and serve responses; they never execute application logic like sending email. A cache would actually *suppress* origin hits, not multiply emails.

Correct — the endpoint violates GET's safety contract, so prefetchers, crawlers, and monitors trigger the regeneration and emails autonomously; a `POST` keeps automated GET traffic from causing side effects.
variants.interviewTip: Distinguish *safe* (no side effects: `GET`, `HEAD`) from *idempotent* (repeat leaves same state: `GET`, `PUT`, `DELETE`). All safe methods are idempotent, but not vice versa — interviewers love asking for that exact Venn diagram.

sections.heading: Response status codes: the server's verdict
paragraphs: Every response opens with a three-digit status code, and its first digit tells you who to blame before you read another byte. 2xx: success (`200 OK`, `201 Created` after a `POST`, `204 No Content` when there's nothing to return). 3xx: redirection (`301` moved permanently, `302` moved temporarily, `304` not modified — your cached copy is still good). 4xx: the client did something wrong. 5xx: the server failed. This grouping is what lets monitoring dashboards and client interceptors react to whole families at once.

The 4xx family is the one interviewers probe. `400` malformed request, `401` not authenticated (who are you?), `403` authenticated but not allowed (I know who you are — no), `404` resource doesn't exist, `409` conflict (e.g. an edit collided with a newer version), `429` too many requests (rate limited).

The 401 vs 403 distinction trips people up constantly, partly because `401`'s official name is the misleading 'Unauthorized' when it actually means *unauthenticated*. The clean mnemonic: 401 means 'log in first'; 403 means 'logging in won't help — you're known and still not allowed.' Getting this right isn't pedantry: client code routinely keys `401` to a token-refresh or login redirect and `403` to a plain denial message, so the wrong code drives the wrong behavior.
sections.summary: The status code is the server's short verdict, and the number's first digit alone tells you who to blame and what to do next.

variants.question: A logged-in user with a valid session tries to open the admin dashboard, but they are not an admin. Which status code should the server return?
options: 403 Forbidden
404 Not Found
500 Internal Server Error
401 Unauthorized
variants.rationale: The user is authenticated (we know who they are) but not authorized (their role doesn't permit this). That is precisely 403 Forbidden. Despite its confusing name, 401 'Unauthorized' actually means unauthenticated.
optionExplanations: Correct — authenticated but lacking permission is 403.
404 is defensible only as a deliberate strategy to hide the resource's existence (GitHub does this for private repos) — but as the straightforward semantic answer, it's wrong.
Nothing failed on the server. 5xx codes mean the server itself errored, which would page an on-call engineer for what is actually normal access control.
401 means the request lacks valid credentials — 'log in and try again'. This user is already logged in; logging in again changes nothing.
variants.interviewTip: Say the mnemonic out loud in interviews: '401 = who are you? 403 = I know who you are, and no.' Bonus points for noting some APIs return 404 to avoid leaking resource existence.

variants.question: An API client calls a protected endpoint but its access token has fully expired, so the server can no longer establish who the caller is. Following HTTP semantics, which status code most precisely signals 'your credentials are missing or invalid — re-authenticate'?
options: 400 Bad Request
401 Unauthorized
429 Too Many Requests
403 Forbidden
variants.rationale: An expired token means the request effectively lacks valid credentials, so the server cannot identify the caller. That is the exact meaning of 401 — despite the word 'Unauthorized', it signals *unauthenticated*: re-present valid credentials and try again.
optionExplanations: 400 is for a syntactically malformed or unparseable request. An expired token is a well-formed request with an authentication problem, not a parsing problem.
Correct — missing or invalid credentials the server can't authenticate is 401; the client should refresh or re-obtain a token.
429 signals rate limiting — too many requests in a window. Token expiry has nothing to do with request volume.
403 means the identity is known but not permitted; here the identity can't even be established, so re-authenticating is the fix, which is 401's message, not 403's.
variants.interviewTip: Flip the primary question's trap: here the credentials are the problem, so it's 401, not 403. Note that 401 responses should include a `WWW-Authenticate` header telling the client how to authenticate.

variants.question: While authenticated, you request another tenant's private document by guessing its ID, and the API returns `404 Not Found` — even though you know the document exists. Why would a well-designed API choose this response deliberately?
options: The server hit an internal routing bug that mapped the request onto a handler that does not exist
The API is simply wrong here — HTTP mandates a `403` whenever a resource exists but access is denied
A `403` would confirm the resource exists; one uniform `404` stops attackers enumerating IDs at all
`404` responses are meaningfully cheaper for the server to generate than `403` responses are to build
variants.rationale: A `403` on a guessed ID leaks information: 'something is here, you just can't see it.' By collapsing 'doesn't exist' and 'exists but private' into one indistinguishable `404`, the API denies attackers an oracle for mapping out private data. The HTTP spec explicitly permits `404` in place of `403` for exactly this reason — GitHub does it for private repositories.
optionExplanations: Nothing malfunctioned — the routing worked and access control ran; the `404` is a deliberate policy choice, not an error in dispatch.
The spec allows a server that wishes to hide a resource's existence to respond `404` instead of `403`; the mandate this option imagines does not exist.
Correct — uniform `404`s make existing-but-forbidden indistinguishable from nonexistent, closing off resource-enumeration attacks.
Both are trivial responses to produce; the choice is driven by information leakage, not compute cost.
variants.interviewTip: Volunteering the security angle — '403 confirms existence, so sensitive APIs return 404 instead' — turns a status-code question into a security answer. Cite GitHub's private-repo behavior as your concrete example.

variants.question: A logged-in user tries to delete a teammate's comment and lacks permission. The server responds `401`, and the SPA — following standard convention — clears the session and redirects to the login page, trapping the user in a re-login loop. Which single change fixes both the semantics and the loop?
options: Return `403 Forbidden` — the user is authenticated but not permitted, so the client shows a denial note
Return `200` with an error flag in the body so the client stops reacting to HTTP status codes altogether
Return `500`, since the delete the user attempted ultimately did not succeed on the server at all
Keep the `401` but have the login page auto-submit the saved credentials so the loop turns invisible
variants.rationale: Clients automate against status codes as a contract: `401` conventionally means 'credentials invalid — re-authenticate,' which is why the SPA nukes the session. The user's credentials are fine; their *role* is insufficient. That is `403`, which client code handles by showing a denial message rather than restarting the auth flow.
optionExplanations: Correct — `403` states 'identity confirmed, permission denied,' so the client's re-auth machinery stays out of it and the loop disappears.
Tunneling errors through `200` breaks caches, monitoring, and every intermediary that reads status codes; it treats the symptom by discarding the contract.
Nothing failed on the server — access control worked exactly as designed. A `5xx` would page on-call for correct behavior.
Auto-submitting login hides the loop while re-authenticating a user whose authentication was never the problem; the wrong code still drives the wrong client behavior.
variants.interviewTip: Frame status codes as a machine-readable contract, not decoration: interceptors key `401` to token-refresh/login flows and `403` to denial UI. Explaining the *client-side consequence* of a wrong code is what separates senior answers.

sections.heading: DNS: from name to address
paragraphs: Computers route packets to IP addresses, not names, so before any connection can open, the human-friendly name must be translated. DNS turns `example.com` into an address like `93.184.216.34`. Your machine first checks local caches (the browser's, the OS's), then asks a resolver — usually run by your ISP or a public provider like `1.1.1.1`. If the resolver doesn't already know, it walks the hierarchy: root servers point it to the `.com` TLD servers, which point to example.com's authoritative nameserver, which returns the actual record. That answer is then cached at every hop on the way back.

Records have types, and knowing a handful covers most real work: `A` maps a name to an IPv4 address, `AAAA` to an IPv6 address, `CNAME` aliases one name to another name (so you follow through to wherever *that* points), `MX` routes mail, and `TXT` holds arbitrary text — frequently domain-ownership proofs and email-authentication policies.

Every record carries a TTL — how many seconds resolvers are allowed to cache it. Low TTLs mean changes propagate fast but generate more lookup traffic; high TTLs are cheaper but slower to update. Crucially, the TTL is baked into the answer *when it's fetched*, so a resolver honors the value it saw, not the value you set later. That's why 'DNS propagation delay' is mostly just caches around the world waiting for their TTLs to expire — and why you lower the TTL well before a planned migration.
sections.summary: DNS turns a name into an address, and the delay you feel after a change is just old cached answers waiting for their TTL to expire.

variants.question: You change your site's A record to point at a new server, but some visitors still reach the old server for hours. Why?
options: The new A record only applies to fresh visitors who have never once loaded the site before
The old server is actively intercepting the traffic that was meant to reach the new one
Resolvers and operating systems cache the DNS answer until the record's TTL finally expires
DNS changes like this one require the visitor's browser to be updated before they take effect
variants.rationale: DNS answers are cached at many layers — the OS, the router, the ISP's resolver — each honoring the TTL that was on the record when it was fetched. Until those caches expire, they keep serving the old IP. This is why you lower the TTL *before* a planned migration.
optionExplanations: DNS has no concept of new vs returning visitors; it's purely name-to-address lookup with caching.
The old server does nothing active — traffic reaches it because cached answers still name its IP.
Correct — layered caching plus TTL is the entire mechanism behind 'propagation delay'.
Browsers have small DNS caches but need no update; the delay lives in resolver caches, not software versions.
variants.interviewTip: The pro move in a systems interview: 'before migrating, drop the TTL to 60 seconds a day in advance, migrate, then raise it back.'

variants.question: You want to point `blog.example.com` at a third-party host that manages its own rotating set of IP addresses, so you never have to update an IP yourself when they change servers. Which DNS record type is designed for this 'alias one name to another name' job?
options: An `MX` record that points `blog.example.com` at the third-party host
A `TXT` record that simply contains the third-party host's domain name
An `A` record that lists all of the host's current IP addresses by hand
A `CNAME` record aliasing `blog.example.com` to the host's own domain
variants.rationale: A `CNAME` aliases one name to another name, so `blog.example.com` resolves by following through to the provider's hostname — and whatever IPs *they* map that name to are used automatically. You never touch an IP, which is exactly the delegation you want.
optionExplanations: `MX` records route email to mail servers; they have nothing to do with resolving a web hostname to an address.
`TXT` holds arbitrary text (like verification strings) and is never followed as an address alias by resolvers doing name resolution.
An `A` record hard-codes specific IPs, so you'd have to edit it every time the provider rotates servers — the opposite of hands-off.
Correct — `CNAME` aliases your name to the provider's name, so their IP changes flow through without you editing anything.
variants.interviewTip: Know the classic `CNAME` gotcha: you can't put a `CNAME` on a zone apex (`example.com` itself) alongside other required records — which is why providers offer `ALIAS`/`ANAME` or flattening for the root domain.

variants.question: The `A` record for `api.example.com` carries a TTL of 86400 (24 hours), and you must cut over to a new IP next Friday with minimal disruption. What is the correct TTL play?
options: On Friday, change the IP and set the TTL to 30 in one edit, so the low TTL takes effect for everyone at once
Lower the TTL well before Friday, let old answers age out of caches, switch the IP, then raise the TTL back
Set the TTL to 0 permanently, so that resolver caches can never become a factor in any future change again
Skip the TTL entirely — it governs only `CNAME` chains, so an `A` change propagates on the resolvers' schedule
variants.rationale: The TTL travels *with* the cached answer: resolvers holding the old record honor the 86400 that was attached when they fetched it, so a TTL you set at cutover time reaches no one who already has the old answer. You must lower the TTL at least one full old-TTL period in advance, so that by Friday every cache holds a short-lived answer that expires quickly after the switch.
optionExplanations: Caches that fetched the record before Friday obey the old 86400 they stored — your new TTL is only seen by resolvers fetching *after* the change, which is exactly the population that didn't need it.
Correct — pre-lowering by at least the old TTL guarantees all caches hold short-lived answers at cutover; raising it afterward restores cheap, low-traffic resolution.
A TTL of 0 (or near-zero) forever means every request pays a fresh lookup — needless latency and resolver load — and some resolvers clamp or ignore extreme values anyway.
TTL applies to every cached record type, `A` included; there is no `CNAME`-only rule, and ignoring it is how you get a day of split traffic.
variants.interviewTip: State the timing rule crisply: 'the TTL you need at cutover must be set at least one old-TTL period beforehand.' Interviewers use this to test whether you understand that caching decisions were made in the past, not at the moment you edit the zone.

variants.question: Users on an IPv6-only mobile carrier (no IPv4 path, no NAT64) report your site never loads, while everyone else is fine. Your zone currently contains just one `A` record for the hostname. Which record type must you add so their devices can resolve an address they can actually reach?
options: A second `A` record carrying a different IPv4 address, added for redundancy
A `TXT` record that publicly announces the site now supports IPv6 clients
An `MX` record that points the hostname at an IPv6-capable mail gateway
An `AAAA` record mapping the hostname to your server's own IPv6 address
variants.rationale: An `A` record answers only IPv4 queries; an IPv6-only client asks for `AAAA` and gets nothing usable back. Publishing an `AAAA` record alongside the `A` record (dual-stack) gives those clients a reachable IPv6 address while IPv4 clients continue using the `A` record.
optionExplanations: More IPv4 addresses cannot help a client with no IPv4 path at all — redundancy within an unreachable family is still unreachable.
`TXT` records are inert text for humans and verification tooling; resolvers never use them to route traffic anywhere.
`MX` records direct *email* delivery for the domain; they play no role in resolving a website's hostname for browsers.
Correct — `AAAA` is the IPv6 counterpart of `A`; adding it lets IPv6-only clients resolve and connect, completing a dual-stack setup.
variants.interviewTip: Pair the record knowledge with the client behavior: dual-stacked browsers race both families via Happy Eyeballs and prefer whichever connects first. Mentioning that turns a flashcard answer into a networking answer.

sections.heading: The DOM: the page as a living tree
paragraphs: When the browser parses HTML, it builds the DOM — a tree of node objects held in memory. The HTML file is the blueprint; the DOM is the standing building. This is the distinction that confuses beginners most: JavaScript never edits your `.html` file on disk. It mutates the in-memory tree, and the browser re-renders to match. View the page source and you see the original blueprint; open DevTools and you see the live tree, which may look completely different after scripts have run.

Every DOM mutation can trigger a chain of work: style recalculation, layout (computing geometry — this is *reflow*), and paint. Touching the DOM is orders of magnitude more expensive than touching plain JavaScript objects, because a single change can invalidate the layout of everything around it. That cost is the entire reason virtual-DOM libraries like React exist: hold a cheap copy of the tree, batch your intended changes, compute the minimal diff, and touch the real DOM as little as possible.

The DOM is also *live*: `document.querySelector` hands you a reference into the tree itself, not a snapshot. Change the node you got back and the page changes with it. Some older APIs go further and return live *collections* (`getElementsByTagName`) that keep updating as the tree changes — a subtlety that bites anyone who loops over one while mutating the page.
sections.summary: The DOM is a live tree the browser draws from, and touching it is slow, so change it as little as possible and batch your updates.

variants.question: Why is repeatedly updating the real DOM inside a loop (e.g. appending 1,000 rows one at a time) considered a performance mistake?
options: Each mutation can force the browser to recalc styles, layout, and paint, so unbatched work grows
JavaScript loops are inherently slow no matter what the body of the loop actually happens to be doing
The DOM turns read-only for the duration of a loop and silently drops every write you attempt
The DOM can only hold a fixed maximum number of elements before it starts to error out on you
variants.rationale: The cost isn't the loop — it's that every insertion can invalidate layout and trigger reflow/repaint. Batching (build a DocumentFragment, append once) or diffing (React) collapses 1,000 potential reflows into one.
optionExplanations: Correct — reflow and repaint are the expensive steps, and unbatched mutations repeat them needlessly.
Plain JS loops execute millions of iterations per second; the loop is innocent, the per-iteration DOM work is guilty.
The DOM is fully writable at any time; nothing is dropped — that's why all 1,000 slow reflows actually happen.
There is no meaningful hard cap; huge DOMs get slow, but they don't error at a limit.
variants.interviewTip: If asked 'why does React exist', anchor your answer here: real-DOM mutations are expensive, so React batches state changes and commits a minimal diff.

variants.question: In a loop over a list, your code writes `el.style.width` to grow an element and then immediately reads `el.offsetHeight` on each iteration, and the page becomes janky. What specific pattern is making this so slow?
options: Reading `offsetHeight` allocates a large fresh copy of the whole DOM each time that it runs
Interleaving a write with a read of a layout property forces a synchronous reflow every pass
`style.width` is actually an invalid property, so the browser keeps retrying the assignment
Reading and writing the DOM in one function is disallowed and gets silently throttled for you
variants.rationale: The browser batches style writes and flushes layout lazily — but reading a geometry property like `offsetHeight` forces it to compute layout *now* to give an accurate answer. Doing that read right after a write, every iteration, defeats batching and triggers a synchronous reflow each time. This is layout thrashing; the fix is to batch all reads, then all writes.
optionExplanations: Reading `offsetHeight` copies nothing; it returns a number. The cost is the forced layout recalculation it triggers, not any allocation.
Correct — write-then-read of a layout property forces a synchronous reflow per iteration, the definition of layout thrashing.
`style.width` is perfectly valid; there is no invalid-property retry loop involved.
Reading and writing the DOM together is fully allowed; nothing is throttled or blocked — it just forces expensive synchronous layouts.
variants.interviewTip: Name the fix crisply: 'batch reads, then batch writes' — or reach for `requestAnimationFrame` / `getBoundingClientRect` measured up front. Saying 'layout thrashing' by name signals real DOM-performance depth.

variants.question: To render 500 search results, a colleague builds each `<li>` inside a detached `DocumentFragment` and appends the fragment to the live `<ul>` once at the end. Why is this dramatically cheaper than appending each `<li>` to the live list as it's built?
options: `DocumentFragment` compresses its child nodes so they take up far less memory once inserted
Fragments are rendered on a background thread, freeing the main thread during construction
A detached fragment isn't in the rendered tree, so its inserts skip layout till one live append
The browser skips the HTML parsing step entirely once the nodes arrive wrapped up in a fragment
variants.rationale: Reflow and repaint are only in play for nodes attached to the rendered document. A detached `DocumentFragment` is off-stage: you can hammer it with hundreds of mutations for free. When the fragment is appended, its children move into the live tree in a single operation, collapsing what could have been hundreds of layout invalidations into one.
optionExplanations: Fragments store perfectly ordinary nodes with no compression; the win is *when* rendering work happens, not how much memory nodes take.
All of this DOM construction runs on the main thread; fragments change the batching of rendering work, not which thread executes it.
Correct — off-tree mutations are invisible to the renderer, so the expensive style/layout/paint pipeline runs once at the single live insertion.
These nodes are built via the DOM API, not parsed from markup — and parsing cost isn't the bottleneck; repeated live-tree layout work is.
variants.interviewTip: Frame `DocumentFragment` as manual batching — 'the same principle React's reconciler automates.' Connecting a vanilla-DOM technique to the framework's reason for existing is a high-signal move.

variants.question: This loop never terminates: `const divs = document.getElementsByTagName('div'); for (let i = 0; i < divs.length; i++) { document.body.appendChild(document.createElement('div')); }` — what property of the DOM explains the hang?
options: `getElementsByTagName` returns a *live* collection, so each new `<div>` grows `divs.length` further
`appendChild` is asynchronous, so the loop body outruns the insertions and the two of them deadlock
Creating elements inside a loop leaks memory until the tab finally dies, which just resembles a hang
`for` loops cannot read `length` off a DOM collection, so the condition always evaluates to `true`
variants.rationale: The DOM is live, and so are the classic collection APIs: `getElementsByTagName` hands back an `HTMLCollection` that reflects the tree *right now*. Every iteration appends a `<div>`, the collection instantly reports one more element, and `i < divs.length` can never become false. A static snapshot — `document.querySelectorAll('div')` or a copied array — breaks the feedback loop.
optionExplanations: Correct — the live `HTMLCollection` updates as the tree changes, so the loop keeps moving its own goalposts; snapshot it first and the loop terminates.
`appendChild` is fully synchronous — the node is in the tree before the next statement runs. There is no async race here, just a self-growing bound.
Memory grows because the loop is infinite, not the other way around; the causal bug is the live collection feeding the loop condition.
Reading `.length` from an `HTMLCollection` works fine anywhere — that's exactly how the loop keeps observing the ever-growing count.
variants.interviewTip: Know which APIs are live and which are static: `getElementsByTagName`/`getElementsByClassName` and `node.children` are live; `querySelectorAll` returns a static `NodeList`. That one-liner defuses a whole family of trick questions.

sections.heading: Cookies, sessions, and tokens: giving HTTP a memory
paragraphs: Because HTTP forgets between requests, continuity has to ride *inside* each request. The oldest mechanism is the cookie: the server sends a `Set-Cookie` header once, the browser stores that small string, and it automatically attaches it back as a `Cookie` header on every future request to that site. Cookies are how the browser 'remembers' who you are without the protocol doing so — the memory lives in a value the client keeps re-presenting.

There are two broad ways to use that cookie. In a *session* scheme, the cookie holds only an opaque session ID; the real data (your user record, your cart) sits in server-side storage keyed by that ID. The server is the source of truth and can revoke a session instantly by deleting it. In a *token* scheme — a JWT is the common example — the cookie or `Authorization: Bearer` header carries a signed, self-contained token that states who you are; the server trusts the signature without a lookup, which scales beautifully but makes instant revocation harder because the token is valid until it expires.

Since a cookie is just a client-held credential, protecting it is critical. `HttpOnly` hides it from JavaScript so a cross-site script can't steal it. `Secure` sends it only over HTTPS. `SameSite` limits when it's attached to cross-site requests, which is a key defense against CSRF. Get these flags wrong and 'remembering the user' quietly becomes 'letting an attacker impersonate the user.'
sections.summary: Stateless HTTP gets a memory when the client re-sends a cookie or token every request, and auth is really just the server trusting and protecting that credential.

variants.question: After you log in, the server sends `Set-Cookie: session=abc123`. On your next request to the same site, how does that cookie get back to the server?
options: The server opens a fresh connection back to your browser to pull the stored cookie out of it again
The browser stores it and attaches it as a `Cookie` header on matching requests to that site
Your app's JavaScript has to read the cookie and manually copy it onto every single outgoing request
The cookie travels only once at login and is thereafter cached server-side for the whole session
variants.rationale: Cookies are the browser's built-in continuity mechanism: once `Set-Cookie` stores a value, the browser resends it as a `Cookie` header on every subsequent request whose domain and path match — no application code required. That automatic re-presentation is exactly how a stateless protocol appears to 'remember' you.
optionExplanations: Servers cannot reach into a browser and pull data out; the flow is client-driven, with the browser choosing to attach the cookie itself.
Correct — the browser stores the cookie and re-sends it automatically on every matching request, which is what gives HTTP its apparent memory.
Manual copying is only needed for tokens kept outside cookies; a real cookie is attached by the browser automatically, and an `HttpOnly` one isn't even readable by JavaScript.
The cookie is sent on the login response and then on every following request; it is not a one-time value cached only on the server.
variants.interviewTip: Say the loop out loud: 'server sets it once, browser resends it every request.' Then mention `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, and `SameSite` to show you know cookies are a security surface, not just a storage bucket.

variants.question: A team runs many stateless API servers behind a load balancer and wants each server to validate a caller's identity without any shared session lookup on every request. Which auth approach fits that goal most directly?
options: A signed, self-contained token (like a JWT) that any server can verify from its signature alone
An opaque session ID that every server resolves by querying one central session store each time
Sticky sessions that pin each user to the single server that first authenticated their login
Basic auth, re-sending the raw username and password on every request for the server to re-check
variants.rationale: A signed token carries the identity claims inside it, so any server holding the verification key can trust the token by checking its signature — no round trip to shared storage. That statelessness is precisely what makes tokens scale across a fleet, at the cost of harder instant revocation.
optionExplanations: Correct — a self-contained signed token is verifiable locally on any server, avoiding a per-request central lookup entirely.
An opaque session ID means nothing on its own, so every server must hit the central store to resolve it — the exact lookup the goal rules out.
Sticky sessions avoid shared lookups by trapping the user on one server, but that reintroduces state and breaks if that server dies — the opposite of stateless scaling.
Basic auth re-checks credentials against the user store on every request, which is both a heavy per-request lookup and a serious security downgrade.
variants.interviewTip: State the trade-off unprompted: tokens scale without shared state but are hard to revoke before expiry; server sessions revoke instantly but need shared storage. Naming both sides is the senior signal.

variants.question: A reviewer flags that a session cookie is set without the `HttpOnly` flag. What concrete risk does adding `HttpOnly` mitigate?
options: It stops the cookie being sent over unencrypted HTTP connections
It blocks page JavaScript from reading the cookie, so injected XSS can't steal it
It prevents the browser from attaching the cookie to a different site's requests
It shrinks the cookie's lifetime so that it silently expires the very instant the browser tab is closed again
variants.rationale: `HttpOnly` makes a cookie invisible to `document.cookie` and all client-side scripting. Its purpose is to blunt cross-site scripting (XSS): even if an attacker injects a script into your page, that script cannot read the session cookie and exfiltrate it, because the value is simply not exposed to JavaScript.
optionExplanations: Restricting a cookie to encrypted connections is the job of the `Secure` flag, not `HttpOnly`.
Correct — `HttpOnly` hides the cookie from JavaScript, so an XSS payload can't read and steal the session value.
Controlling whether a cookie rides along on cross-site requests is what `SameSite` governs; `HttpOnly` doesn't decide when the cookie is sent.
Cookie lifetime is set by `Expires`/`Max-Age`; `HttpOnly` says nothing about when a cookie expires.
variants.interviewTip: Keep the flag trio straight: `HttpOnly` (no JS access, anti-XSS), `Secure` (HTTPS only), `SameSite` (cross-site sending, anti-CSRF). Interviewers often ask you to map each flag to the attack it counters.

variants.question: A colleague argues that stateless JWTs are strictly better than server-side sessions 'because there's nothing to store.' What is the most important caveat to raise?
options: JWTs can't carry user identity, so you still need a session store
JWTs must be re-issued on every single request, which cancels out the entire performance benefit they offer
A self-contained JWT stays valid until it expires, making instant revocation hard
JWTs only work over HTTP/2, so older clients silently fall back to server-side sessions regardless anyway
variants.rationale: The very property that makes a JWT convenient — the server trusts it from its signature without any lookup — is what makes revocation awkward. Once issued, the token is accepted until it expires, so 'log this user out everywhere right now' or 'ban this compromised token' requires extra machinery like short lifetimes plus refresh tokens, or a denylist that reintroduces the state you were trying to avoid.
optionExplanations: JWTs are designed to carry identity claims in their payload; that's their whole point, so this is backwards.
A JWT is issued once and presented on many requests; it is not re-minted per request, so no such cost exists.
Correct — a signed token is valid until expiry, so revoking it early requires extra mechanisms and is the key trade-off against server sessions.
JWTs are just signed strings carried in a header or cookie; they are independent of the HTTP version in use.
variants.interviewTip: When someone calls a design 'strictly better,' probe the trade-off. Here: statelessness buys scale but costs revocation. Mentioning short-lived access tokens plus refresh tokens shows you know the standard mitigation.

sections.heading: Caching: making the web fast (and stale)
paragraphs: The fastest request is the one you never make. Caching lets a response be reused instead of re-fetched, and it happens at many layers: the browser's own cache, shared proxy or CDN caches near the user, and caches inside the server. The server steers all of this with response headers, chiefly `Cache-Control` — for example `Cache-Control: max-age=3600` tells caches a copy stays fresh for one hour, while `no-store` forbids caching entirely and `private` limits it to the end user's browser.

When a cached copy's freshness runs out, the client doesn't have to blindly re-download it — it can *revalidate*. The server can tag a response with an `ETag` (a fingerprint of the content) or a `Last-Modified` date. On the next request the client sends that value back in `If-None-Match` or `If-Modified-Since`; if nothing changed, the server replies `304 Not Modified` with an empty body, and the client reuses what it already has. You pay a round trip but skip the download.

This is also where 'why is my change not showing up?' bugs come from. A long `max-age` on an HTML file means users keep seeing the old page until the cache expires. The standard fix is a *cache-busting* filename: name built assets `app.9f2c.js` with a content hash, cache them for a year, and change the filename whenever the content changes — so a new deploy is a new URL that no cache has seen.
sections.summary: Caching reuses responses to skip work, `Cache-Control` and `ETag` govern how long and how it's revalidated, and stale content is the price you manage with expiry and hashed filenames.

variants.question: A response includes `Cache-Control: max-age=3600`. What does that instruct caches to do?
options: Store this copy but revalidate it with the origin before every reuse
Keep this copy for exactly 3600 separate requests, after which it is discarded regardless of time
Reuse this copy as fresh, with no call to the server, for up to 3600 seconds
Refuse to store this response at all, as max-age disables caching
variants.rationale: `max-age=3600` declares the response fresh for 3600 seconds. While it's fresh, a cache serves it directly with no call to the origin at all — that's the speed win. Only after it goes stale must the cache revalidate or re-fetch.
optionExplanations: Revalidating before every reuse is what `no-cache` requires; `max-age` explicitly lets the cache skip the server while the copy is still fresh.
`max-age` counts seconds of freshness, not a number of requests; the unit is time, not hit count.
Correct — for 3600 seconds the copy is fresh and reused directly, with no request to the origin server.
Refusing to store the response is what `no-store` does; `max-age` does the opposite and enables reuse.
variants.interviewTip: Distinguish `no-cache` (store it, but revalidate every time before use) from `no-store` (never store it at all). The names are counterintuitive, and mixing them up is a classic tell.

variants.question: A cached CSS file has just gone stale. The browser sends its stored `ETag` back in an `If-None-Match` header, and the server replies `304 Not Modified`. What does the browser do next?
options: Re-download the entire full CSS file, because a 304 signals that the cached copy is no longer usable
Reuse its existing cached copy, since a 304 confirms nothing changed and skips the download
Discard the cached copy and render the page with no styles at all until a fresh copy arrives later on
Send the request a second time without the `ETag` so the server returns the file body in full again
variants.rationale: A `304 Not Modified` is the server saying 'your `ETag` matches — nothing changed.' The response carries no body, so the browser keeps and reuses the copy it already has. You spend one small round trip to confirm freshness but avoid re-downloading the file's bytes.
optionExplanations: A 304 means the opposite of unusable — it confirms the cached copy is still valid, so no re-download happens.
Correct — 304 confirms the content is unchanged, so the browser reuses its cached copy and skips downloading the body.
Nothing is discarded; the whole point of revalidation is to keep the existing copy when it's confirmed current.
Re-requesting without the `ETag` would waste the revalidation; the browser already got its answer and reuses the cache.
variants.interviewTip: Frame revalidation as 'pay a round trip, skip the download.' Mention that an `ETag` is a content fingerprint while `Last-Modified` is a timestamp — `ETag` is more precise when content can change without the clock advancing meaningfully.

variants.question: You deploy a bug fix, but users keep running the old JavaScript for hours. The file is served as `app.js` with `Cache-Control: max-age=31536000` (one year). What's the standard fix so future deploys take effect immediately?
options: Include a content hash in each asset's filename so a changed file ships as a brand-new URL
Drop the cache lifetime to zero on every asset so nothing is ever cached across page loads
Ask users to hard-refresh after each deploy, since long-lived caches can't be worked around
Move the JavaScript inline into the HTML so it can never be cached separately by the browser
variants.rationale: A year-long cache on a stable filename means the browser won't even ask about `app.js` until 2027. The fix is cache-busting: build the file as `app.[hash].js` where the hash reflects its contents. When the code changes the hash changes, producing a new URL no cache has ever seen — so it downloads immediately — while unchanged files keep their old hashed URL and stay cached for a year.
optionExplanations: Correct — hashing the filename turns a changed asset into a new URL, so caches fetch it fresh while unchanged assets stay cached long-term.
Zero-lifetime caching throws away the entire performance benefit; you'd re-download unchanged assets on every visit for no reason.
Relying on users to hard-refresh is not a fix — most never will, and the whole point is to make deploys automatic.
Inlining every script bloats the HTML and forfeits caching of code that rarely changes; it treats the symptom by making caching impossible.
variants.interviewTip: Name the pattern 'cache-busting via content-hashed filenames' and note the combo: long `max-age` plus `immutable` on hashed assets, but a short or revalidated cache on the HTML that references them, since the HTML is what points at the new hashes.

variants.question: An API sends bank-balance JSON with `Cache-Control: private, no-store`. Why is `private` here not enough on its own, making `no-store` the important part?
options: `private` blocks shared caches but still lets the user's own browser store the balance locally
`private` applies only to images, so JSON responses ignore it
`private` and `no-store` are exact synonyms here, so including both is purely redundant defensiveness anyway
`private` forces revalidation on every single request, which on its own already guarantees nothing is stored
variants.rationale: `private` only means 'shared caches like CDNs and proxies must not store this' — it explicitly permits the end user's own browser cache to keep a copy. For a sensitive balance that could linger on a shared machine, you want `no-store`, which forbids writing the response to *any* cache at all. `private` narrows who may cache; `no-store` says no one may.
optionExplanations: Correct — `private` still allows the user's own browser to cache the response; `no-store` is what forbids storing it anywhere.
`private` is not media-type specific; it applies to any response, JSON included, so this reasoning is wrong.
They differ meaningfully: `private` restricts *which* caches may store it, `no-store` forbids storing entirely — not synonyms.
Forcing revalidation is `no-cache`'s behavior, not `private`'s, and revalidation still involves storing a copy to revalidate.
variants.interviewTip: Keep the axis clear: `private` vs `public` answers *who* may cache; `no-store` vs storable answers *whether* anyone may. For secrets you want `no-store`; `private` alone leaves a copy on the user's disk.

sections.heading: HTTPS and TLS: trust on an open wire
paragraphs: Plain HTTP travels in the clear: anyone between you and the server — a café's Wi-Fi, an ISP, a compromised router — can read and even alter it. HTTPS is just HTTP running inside a TLS-encrypted channel, and it delivers three things at once: *confidentiality* (eavesdroppers see only ciphertext), *integrity* (tampering is detected), and *authentication* (you're really talking to the site you named, not an impostor).

That last guarantee comes from certificates. A server presents a certificate — its public key plus its domain name — signed by a Certificate Authority the browser already trusts. The browser checks the signature chains up to a trusted root, that the certificate covers the domain you asked for, and that it hasn't expired or been revoked. If any check fails you get the scary full-page warning, because a bad certificate is exactly what a man-in-the-middle attack looks like.

The TLS handshake sets this up before any HTTP is sent. Layered on an established TCP connection, the client and server agree on a cipher, the server proves it owns the certificate's private key, and they derive a shared symmetric key using asymmetric crypto — after which the fast symmetric key encrypts the actual traffic. TLS 1.3 trimmed this to a single round trip, which is why modern HTTPS adds far less latency than its reputation suggests.
sections.summary: HTTPS wraps HTTP in TLS to get confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity, and the certificate is what proves you're talking to the real site rather than an impostor.

variants.question: Beyond encrypting traffic, what critical guarantee does a valid TLS certificate provide?
options: It authenticates the server, proving you're connected to the real domain and not an impostor
It compresses the response body so that encrypted pages will transfer faster than plain HTTP ones do
It guarantees the server's application code is free of bugs and vulnerabilities
It hides your IP from the server so the site can never tell who is connecting
variants.rationale: Encryption alone would be useless if you'd encrypted a conversation with an attacker. The certificate authenticates the server: because it's signed by a CA the browser trusts and it names the domain you requested, you gain confidence you're talking to the genuine site, not a man-in-the-middle. Confidentiality plus authenticity is the point.
optionExplanations: Correct — the certificate proves the server's identity, so you know the encrypted channel is with the real site and not an impostor.
TLS does not compress bodies; that's an unrelated concern, and past TLS-level compression was actually removed for security reasons.
A certificate says nothing about code quality; a fully patched site and a buggy one can both hold valid certificates.
The server still sees your IP — it has to, to send packets back; certificates authenticate the server, not anonymize the client.
variants.interviewTip: List all three properties — confidentiality, integrity, authenticity — and stress that authenticity is what defeats a man-in-the-middle. Many candidates say 'HTTPS = encryption' and stop, missing the identity half.

variants.question: During a TLS connection setup, what is the browser fundamentally verifying when it validates the server's certificate?
options: That the response body has not been modified by any proxy that sits between the client and server
That the certificate is signed by a trusted CA and actually covers the requested domain
That the server is geographically located in the very same country as the person connecting to it
That the user already has an account on the site and has previously entered valid login credentials
variants.rationale: Certificate validation is an identity check: the browser confirms the certificate chains up to a Certificate Authority in its trust store, that it lists the exact domain the user asked for, and that it's currently valid (not expired or revoked). Passing all three is what lets the browser believe the server is who it claims to be.
optionExplanations: Body integrity is enforced continuously by TLS's per-record authentication, not by the one-time certificate check at handshake.
Correct — validation checks the CA signature chain, that the certificate covers the requested domain, and that it's still valid.
Certificates encode domain identity, not physical location; geography plays no role in validation.
User login is an application-layer step that happens after TLS; the certificate authenticates the server to the client, not the user to the server.
variants.interviewTip: Enumerate the checks — trusted signing chain, domain match, not expired/revoked — and note that a mismatch on any one triggers the browser warning. Interviewers use cert-warning scenarios to see if you know what's actually being validated.

variants.question: Why can't a passive attacker who records an entire HTTPS session simply replay the captured bytes later to read the plaintext, given they saw the whole handshake?
options: The handshake derives a per-session key the attacker never sees, so captured bytes stay ciphertext
HTTPS traffic is stored only within the browser's own memory and is wiped the instant the tab is closed
The server refuses to accept any connection at all that reuses an IP address it has seen before recently
Captured TLS bytes automatically self-destruct after just a few minutes and then become unreadable noise
variants.rationale: The handshake uses asymmetric cryptography to let both sides agree on a symmetric session key without ever transmitting it in a form the eavesdropper can use — modern key exchanges (ephemeral Diffie-Hellman) mean the secret is never sent on the wire at all. The attacker sees the negotiation but not the resulting key, so the recorded application data remains ciphertext they can't decrypt.
optionExplanations: Correct — the session key is derived, never transmitted usably, so an eavesdropper who saw every byte still lacks the key to decrypt the traffic.
Where the browser stores plaintext is irrelevant to a wire attacker; the protection is the key the attacker never obtains, not memory hygiene.
TLS security doesn't rest on refusing repeated IPs; connections from the same address are entirely normal and still secure.
Captured bytes don't decay; they'd be perfectly readable if the attacker had the key — which is exactly what they lack.
variants.interviewTip: Drop the term 'forward secrecy': with ephemeral Diffie-Hellman, even stealing the server's long-term private key later won't decrypt past sessions. That's a strong signal you understand *why* the key exchange is designed the way it is.

variants.question: A user visits `https://example.com` and gets a full-page 'Your connection is not private' warning. Which situation would legitimately trigger that certificate error?
options: The certificate was issued for `example.net`, so it doesn't match the domain
The page loads slowly because the server is far away and overloaded
The site uses a `POST` form without any CSRF token protecting it
The server returned a `500` error for the one specific page the user happened to be attempting to open
variants.rationale: The certificate warning is about identity, not availability or app logic. A certificate that names `example.net` cannot vouch for `example.com`, so the browser can't confirm it's talking to the real site — which is indistinguishable from an impostor presenting the wrong certificate, hence the full-page block. Expiry, an untrusted issuer, or a revoked certificate trigger the same class of warning.
optionExplanations: Correct — a domain mismatch means the certificate can't authenticate the requested site, which is exactly what the browser warning guards against.
Slowness and load are performance issues; they don't affect certificate validity and never produce this warning.
Missing CSRF protection is an application-security gap unrelated to TLS; it wouldn't trigger a certificate error.
A `500` is a server-side application error returned *over* a valid TLS connection; the certificate itself is still fine.
variants.interviewTip: Sort certificate errors (domain mismatch, expired, untrusted issuer, revoked) from HTTP errors (`4xx`/`5xx`). The former block before any HTTP flows; the latter arrive as normal responses over a working TLS channel.

sections.heading: CORS and the same-origin policy: why the browser says no
paragraphs: By default the browser enforces the *same-origin policy*: JavaScript on `https://app.com` may freely read responses from `https://app.com`, but is blocked from reading responses fetched from a different origin. An origin is the exact triple of scheme, host, and port — `https://app.com` and `https://api.app.com` are different origins, as are `http` and `https` versions of the same host. This rule exists so a malicious page can't quietly use *your* logged-in cookies to read your email or bank data in the background.

CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is the controlled exception. A server that *wants* to be called from another origin opts in with response headers, chiefly `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`. The crucial subtlety: CORS is enforced by the browser, for browser JavaScript, on the *response*. The request often still reaches the server and runs; the browser simply refuses to hand the response back to the page unless the origin is allowed. That's why tools like `curl` and your backend, which aren't browsers, never hit CORS at all.

For requests that could change data or carry unusual headers, the browser sends a *preflight* first — an `OPTIONS` request asking 'may I send a `PUT` with a `Content-Type: application/json` header from this origin?' Only if the server answers with the matching `Access-Control-Allow-*` headers does the browser send the real request. This is why a mysterious `OPTIONS` call appears in the network tab before your actual `POST`, and why a CORS misconfiguration often looks like a request that 'never fires.'
sections.summary: The same-origin policy stops one site's JavaScript from reading another's responses, and CORS is the server's explicit opt-in — enforced by the browser on the response, with a preflight for anything risky.

variants.question: Your frontend on `https://app.com` calls an API on `https://api.other.com` and the browser console shows a CORS error, yet the server logs show the request arrived and succeeded. What is actually happening?
options: The request failed to leave the browser, so that server log entry is from another client
CORS errors mean the server rejected the request before running any handler code
The request reached the server, but the browser blocked the page from reading the response
The browser corrupted the response body in transit, so the server's success log is just misleading
variants.rationale: CORS is a browser-side gate on the *response*, not a server-side rejection. The cross-origin request was sent and the server handled it, but because the response lacked an `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header permitting `https://app.com`, the browser refused to expose the response to your JavaScript — surfacing as a console error even though the server succeeded.
optionExplanations: The server log proves the request left the browser and arrived; CORS blocks the response, not the outbound request.
CORS doesn't stop the server from running; the handler executed (that's your log), and the block happens afterward in the browser.
Correct — the request ran server-side, but the browser withheld the response from the page because the origin wasn't allowed.
Nothing was corrupted; the body was fine — the browser simply refused to hand it to the page for lacking CORS headers.
variants.interviewTip: Emphasize where enforcement lives: 'CORS is the browser protecting the user, applied to the response.' Add that `curl` or a server-to-server call sees no CORS at all, which explains why the same endpoint 'works in Postman' but not in the browser.

variants.question: What is the same-origin policy fundamentally designed to prevent?
options: A server from accepting requests that originate from any domain at all other than its own registered one
One site's JavaScript from reading another origin's responses via the user's credentials
A page from ever loading images, scripts, or stylesheets hosted anywhere on a third-party domain at all
Two browser tabs open to two different sites from running their own JavaScript at the very same time
variants.rationale: The same-origin policy is a client-side protection for the user: it stops a page at one origin from scripting reads of another origin's responses while riding the user's automatically-sent cookies. Without it, any site you visited could silently fetch and read your logged-in bank or email pages in the background.
optionExplanations: Servers can accept requests from anywhere; the policy constrains what browser JavaScript may *read*, not what servers may receive.
Correct — it blocks one origin's scripts from reading another origin's responses that ride the user's ambient credentials.
Cross-origin images, scripts, and stylesheets load freely; the policy restricts programmatic reading of responses, not embedding resources.
Tabs run their JavaScript concurrently without issue; the policy isolates data access between origins, not execution timing.
variants.interviewTip: Frame it as protecting the user, not the server, and note the loophole it closes: cookies are sent automatically cross-site, so without the policy any page could read your authenticated data. That framing explains why CORS is opt-in per response.

variants.question: Before your app's cross-origin `PUT` request with a JSON body fires, the network tab shows an `OPTIONS` request to the same URL. What is that `OPTIONS` call doing?
options: It's a CORS preflight asking the server whether this cross-origin PUT with these headers is allowed
It's the browser retrying the PUT a very first time using a safer method in case the PUT gets rejected
It's a health check that the browser runs against every single endpoint before sending any request to it
It's the server redirecting the PUT to OPTIONS because all JSON bodies must be negotiated well in advance
variants.rationale: A `PUT` carrying `Content-Type: application/json` isn't a 'simple' request, so the browser sends a CORS preflight — an automatic `OPTIONS` request that asks the server, via `Access-Control-Request-Method` and `-Headers`, whether this origin may send that method with those headers. Only if the server responds with matching `Access-Control-Allow-*` headers does the browser send the real `PUT`.
optionExplanations: Correct — the `OPTIONS` is a preflight checking whether the server permits this cross-origin method and headers before the real request goes out.
It's not a retry; the browser hasn't sent the `PUT` yet — the preflight is a permission check that must pass first.
There's no universal per-endpoint health check; the `OPTIONS` appears specifically because this is a non-simple cross-origin request.
The server isn't redirecting anything; the browser itself initiates the preflight before it will send the `PUT`.
variants.interviewTip: Know what makes a request 'non-simple' and thus preflighted: methods beyond GET/POST/HEAD, custom headers, or a `Content-Type` like `application/json`. Mentioning `Access-Control-Max-Age` to cache the preflight shows you've optimized this in practice.

variants.question: A backend team 'fixes' CORS by reflecting any incoming `Origin` back in `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` and also setting `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. Why is that dangerous?
options: It makes every response larger, so the CORS headers slow the API
It effectively lets any site make credentialed requests and read your users' responses
It disables the preflight entirely, so browsers stop sending OPTIONS and cross-origin caching then breaks
It only permits same-origin calls, so all legitimate cross-origin frontends will now be blocked instead
variants.rationale: Reflecting the caller's origin means *every* origin is allowed, and pairing that with `Allow-Credentials: true` tells the browser it may send the user's cookies and expose the response cross-origin. Together they dismantle the same-origin protection: any malicious site can now make authenticated requests as your logged-in user and read the results — precisely the attack the policy exists to stop.
optionExplanations: A few extra header bytes are negligible; the danger is a security hole, not response size or speed.
Correct — reflecting any origin plus allowing credentials lets any site make authenticated requests and read responses as your logged-in users.
Preflight still happens for non-simple requests; the misconfiguration weakens security rather than turning `OPTIONS` off.
It does the opposite of restricting to same-origin — it opens the API to all origins, which is the whole problem.
variants.interviewTip: Call out the specific combination: wildcard/reflected origin *plus* `Allow-Credentials: true` is the dangerous pairing. Note the spec forbids a literal `*` with credentials for this reason, which is why teams reach for reflection — and reintroduce the hole.

sections.heading: REST and JSON APIs: resources, verbs, and payloads
paragraphs: A REST API models your data as *resources* addressed by URLs, and uses HTTP methods as the verbs acting on them. The URL names the thing (a noun): `/users` is the collection, `/users/42` is one user. The method says what to do: `GET /users/42` reads it, `POST /users` creates a new one, `PUT`/`PATCH /users/42` updates it, and `DELETE /users/42` removes it. That mapping of methods to create-read-update-delete is why people say 'HTTP verbs are CRUD.'

The convention is to keep URLs as nouns and let the method carry the action, so `POST /users/42/deactivate` is more RESTful expressed as an action on a resource than an RPC-style `GET /deactivateUser?id=42`. Good APIs also lean on the status-code families you already know: `201 Created` after a successful `POST`, `204 No Content` after a `DELETE`, `404` for a missing resource, `400` for a malformed body. The HTTP semantics you learned earlier *are* the API contract.

The payload is almost always JSON — a compact, language-neutral format of objects, arrays, strings, numbers, and booleans. The client signals what it's sending with `Content-Type: application/json` and what it wants back with `Accept: application/json`. Because JSON maps cleanly onto the data structures of nearly every language, both a browser and a Python backend can serialize and parse the same `{ "id": 42, "name": "Ada" }` without agreeing on anything beyond the format itself.
sections.summary: REST addresses data as resources by URL and uses HTTP methods as CRUD verbs, and JSON is the neutral payload both sides serialize into and parse out of.

variants.question: In a REST API, which request best expresses 'create a new user'?
options: `GET /users/create` with the new user's fields passed as query-string params
`PUT /createUser` with the user object attached, since PUT is the method for new records
`POST /users` with the new user's data sent as a JSON body in the request payload itself
`DELETE /users` with the new user's data, treating creation as removing an empty slot
variants.rationale: REST names resources with nouns and lets the method carry the action. Creating a new member of the `/users` collection is a `POST` to that collection, with the new user's fields in a JSON body. The server assigns an ID and typically responds `201 Created` with a `Location` header pointing at the new resource.
optionExplanations: `GET` must be safe and never create anything, and stuffing creation into a `/create` verb-URL abandons the resource model entirely.
`PUT` replaces a resource at a *known* URL; a brand-new user has no URL yet, and `/createUser` is an RPC verb, not a resource.
Correct — `POST /users` with a JSON body creates a new member of the collection, the canonical REST creation pattern.
`DELETE` removes a resource; framing creation as deletion inverts the method's meaning entirely.
variants.interviewTip: Recite the CRUD-to-verb map — POST create, GET read, PUT/PATCH update, DELETE remove — and note the follow-up: `POST` returns `201 Created` with a `Location` header. That detail shows you know the full request/response contract, not just the verb.

variants.question: A colleague proposes the endpoint `GET /getUserOrders?userId=42&action=fetch`. What's the core REST design problem with it?
options: It should be a `POST`, because any endpoint at all that reads data from a database has to send a body
It puts an action verb in the URL rather than a resource; `GET /users/42/orders` is cleaner
It's perfectly fine as written; REST places no constraints on how any endpoint URLs may be named or built
It uses a query string, and REST strictly forbids query parameters anywhere at all within any request URL
variants.rationale: REST wants URLs to identify resources (nouns) while the HTTP method supplies the verb. `getUserOrders` and `action=fetch` bake the verb into the path, duplicating what `GET` already says. The resource-oriented form is `GET /users/42/orders` — a `GET` on user 42's orders collection — which reads cleanly and leans on HTTP semantics instead of reinventing them.
optionExplanations: Reads use `GET`, which has no body; requiring a body to read data misunderstands how `GET` works.
Correct — the URL encodes an action verb rather than naming a resource; `GET /users/42/orders` expresses the same thing the RESTful way.
REST is precisely a set of conventions about resource-oriented URLs; 'anything goes' is the opposite of the style.
