Query strings are perfectly RESTful for filtering, sorting, and pagination; they're not forbidden — the verb-in-URL is the real issue.
variants.interviewTip: State the rule as 'nouns in the URL, verbs in the method.' Then note query strings are still fine for filtering and pagination (`/users/42/orders?status=open&page=2`) — so you distinguish a genuine REST smell from a false one.

variants.question: A client `POST`s JSON to an API but the server rejects it with `415 Unsupported Media Type`. Which missing or wrong request detail most directly causes this?
options: The `Content-Type` header doesn't declare `application/json`, so the body isn't parsed as JSON
The `Accept` header is entirely absent, so the server can't tell which format the client wants back in reply
The JSON body is syntactically invalid, which is exactly what a `415` status specifically reports to the client
The request omitted an authorization token, and `415` is the way the server signals missing credentials
variants.rationale: `415 Unsupported Media Type` is about the format of the *request body*. It fires when the `Content-Type` the client declares isn't one the endpoint accepts — typically because it's missing or set to something other than `application/json`, so the server declines to interpret the payload as JSON. The fix is to send `Content-Type: application/json`.
optionExplanations: Correct — `415` means the declared request media type isn't supported, usually a missing or wrong `Content-Type` on a JSON body.
`Accept` describes the desired *response* format; a mismatch there yields `406 Not Acceptable`, not `415`.
Malformed JSON that the server tried to parse would surface as `400 Bad Request`, not a media-type error.
Missing credentials are `401`; `415` speaks only to the body's media type, not authentication.
variants.interviewTip: Separate the two content headers: `Content-Type` describes what you're sending (mismatch → `415`), `Accept` describes what you want back (mismatch → `406`). Nailing that pairing is a clean way to show you read HTTP as a contract.

variants.question: Why is JSON such a common choice for API payloads exchanged between, say, a browser frontend and a Python backend?
options: JSON is encrypted entirely by default, so payloads sent as JSON don't need HTTPS to stay confidential
It's a language-neutral text format that maps cleanly onto nearly every language's data structures
JSON payloads are always smaller than any other format at all, so they minimize bandwidth in every case
Only JavaScript can ever produce JSON, which guarantees both ends of the API must use the same runtime
variants.rationale: JSON's value is neutrality: it's plain text describing objects, arrays, strings, numbers, and booleans — structures that virtually every language can serialize to and parse from. A browser's JavaScript and a Python backend never have to share a runtime or a schema library; they only have to agree on JSON, and each side maps it onto its own native types.
optionExplanations: JSON is not encrypted at all; confidentiality comes from HTTPS wrapping the transfer, entirely independent of the payload format.
Correct — JSON is a neutral text format that both ends can serialize to and parse from using their own native data structures.
JSON isn't always smallest — binary formats like Protocol Buffers are more compact; JSON trades some size for human readability and ubiquity.
Despite the name, JSON is produced and consumed by essentially every language; it doesn't tie either end to a JavaScript runtime.
variants.interviewTip: Sell JSON as neutrality and ubiquity, not raw efficiency. If pushed on performance, mention that binary formats like Protocol Buffers or MessagePack are smaller and faster — a fair trade-off to raise when payload size actually matters.

sections.heading: Putting it together: the life of a page load
paragraphs: Full circle — and now every piece has a name. You press Enter. DNS resolves the name to an IP (checking caches first). The browser opens a TCP connection and, for HTTPS, runs a TLS handshake over it to encrypt the channel and verify the server's certificate. Then it sends an HTTP `GET`, carrying headers like `Cookie` and `Accept`. The server checks credentials, maybe consults a cache, and responds with a status code, headers (including `Cache-Control`), and an HTML payload.

The browser parses that HTML into the DOM, discovers linked CSS and JS, and fetches those as more HTTP requests — some served instantly from the local cache, the rest from the network. It combines styles with the DOM to compute layout, paints the pixels, and then JavaScript hooks into the tree to make the page interactive. A second visit is far faster because DNS is cached, the connection is reused, and shared assets come straight from the HTTP cache.

Every pillar above this foundation is a deepening of one step in that chain: HTTPS and CORS govern how the request is trusted, caching decides what's re-fetched, cookies and tokens carry identity, REST shapes the request and response, React and CSS live in the render/DOM phase, Next.js decides where the HTML gets generated, Node is the server answering, and databases are where the server gets its facts.
sections.summary: Loading a page is one clear chain — resolve, connect, request, parse, paint — and everything you'll learn later just deepens one of those steps.

variants.question: Put these page-load steps in the order they occur: (A) browser paints pixels, (B) DNS lookup, (C) HTML parsed into DOM, (D) HTTP request sent.
options: B → C → D → A
C → B → D → A
B → D → C → A
D → B → A → C
variants.rationale: You can't send a request without an IP (DNS first), can't parse a response you haven't requested (request before parse), and can't paint a tree you haven't built (parse before paint). B → D → C → A.
optionExplanations: There is no HTML to parse before the HTTP response arrives — the request must come before parsing.
Parsing HTML first is impossible; the HTML only exists client-side after DNS + request + response.
Correct — resolve the name, send the request, parse the response into the DOM, paint.
The request can't be addressed before DNS gives you an IP, and painting can't precede having a DOM to paint.
variants.interviewTip: 'Walk me through what happens when you hit Enter on a URL' is a top-5 interview question. Practice narrating this chain in under 90 seconds, then offer to zoom into any step.

variants.question: For an HTTPS page load, order these four events as they actually occur: (W) TLS handshake completes, (X) browser establishes the TCP connection, (Y) server sends back the HTML response, (Z) browser sends the HTTP GET request.
options: W → X → Z → Y
X → Z → W → Y
Z → X → W → Y
X → W → Z → Y
variants.rationale: TCP is established first (X), then the TLS handshake runs on top of that connection to secure it (W), and only over the now-encrypted channel does the browser send the HTTP GET (Z), after which the server returns the HTML (Y). You can't encrypt a connection you haven't opened, and you can't send an HTTPS request before the channel is secured.
optionExplanations: TLS cannot complete before a TCP connection exists to carry the handshake; the connection must come first.
This puts the request before TLS finishes, meaning the HTTP GET would travel unencrypted — which defeats HTTPS and isn't how the browser sequences it.
This sends the GET before TCP is even established, which is impossible — there is no connection to send over yet.
Correct — TCP connect, then TLS handshake over it, then the encrypted GET, then the HTML response.
variants.interviewTip: For HTTPS, remember the layering: TCP first, TLS on top, HTTP inside. Bonus depth: mention that TLS 1.3 cut the handshake to one round trip, and that QUIC/HTTP/3 folds transport and crypto setup together to save round trips.

variants.question: On a cold page load, order these four events as they actually occur: (P) the render-blocking stylesheet is fetched, (Q) the resolver returns the site's IP address, (R) the first pixels are painted, (S) the HTML response begins arriving.
options: Q → P → S → R
Q → S → P → R
S → Q → P → R
Q → S → R → P
variants.rationale: DNS must resolve before anything can be requested (Q first). The stylesheet's URL lives inside the HTML, so the browser can't discover — let alone fetch — it until the HTML starts arriving and being parsed (S before P). And because the stylesheet is render-blocking, the browser withholds first paint until that CSS is in hand (P before R). Q → S → P → R.
optionExplanations: The browser learns the stylesheet exists from a `<link>` tag in the HTML; it cannot fetch a URL it hasn't seen, so P cannot precede S.
Correct — resolve the name, receive the HTML, discover and fetch the render-blocking CSS, then paint.
No HTML can arrive before the browser has an IP to connect to — DNS strictly precedes the response.
Painting before a *render-blocking* stylesheet arrives is exactly what 'render-blocking' rules out; the browser would risk a flash of unstyled content, so it waits.
variants.interviewTip: Use the phrase 'render-blocking' deliberately and note the browser's preload scanner can *start* the CSS fetch early during parsing — but paint still waits on it. That nuance shows you know the pipeline, not just the flashcard order.

variants.question: A user's first-ever visit to your site takes about 3 seconds, but clicking through to a second page moments later takes about 300 ms. Which pair of mechanisms best explains most of the reclaimed time?
options: The server simply renders faster once it recognizes the returning browser's user-agent string
The second page just contains far less HTML, and raw HTML byte size dominates the total load time
DNS is already cached and the TCP+TLS connection is reused, while shared assets come from the HTTP cache
After the first page the browser drops HTTP and speaks raw TCP to the server, skipping protocol overhead
variants.rationale: The first visit pays every setup cost: DNS resolution, TCP handshake, TLS negotiation, and a cold download of every asset. The second navigation skips nearly all of it — the OS/resolver cache answers DNS instantly, the still-warm connection is reused, and the stylesheet, scripts, and fonts shared across pages come from the local HTTP cache. Only the new page's HTML (and any unique assets) touches the network.
optionExplanations: Servers don't get faster by recognizing a user agent; the savings are on the client and connection side, not in server rendering speed.
HTML is typically a small slice of total transfer; the dominant first-visit costs are connection setup and the cold asset downloads that the second navigation avoids.
Correct — cached DNS, a reused TCP+TLS connection, and HTTP-cached shared assets eliminate the setup and re-download costs that dominated the first load.
HTTP is never abandoned for raw TCP; subsequent requests still speak HTTP — they're just carried over an already-established, already-encrypted connection.
variants.interviewTip: Enumerate the caches by layer — DNS cache, warm connection, HTTP asset cache — and you've implicitly answered the follow-up 'so what would you optimize for first-time visitors?' (fewer round trips, preconnect, caching headers).
